title: Rceattle — Claude Code guide
text: Rceattle (v4.7.0, GPL) fits CEATTLE single- multi-species, climate-linked, age-structured stock assessment model. likelihood TMB / C++ model (src/TMB/); everything around (data prep, fitting, projection, MSE, diagnostics, plotting) R.

title: Rceattle — Claude Code guide
text: TMB package, C++ must compiled R can run. Toolchain: prefix R compile/check commands export PATH=/usr/bin:$PATH (system toolchain first — avoids Homebrew clang/gfortran shadowing TMB build). repo’s sessions consistently. Editing src/TMB/*.cpp *.hpp effect reload — load_all() recompiles via src/TMB/compile.R; add compile = FALSE R-changes. Compiled artifacts (*.o ~77 MB, *.) gitignored — never commit . Tests run NOT_CRAN=true. run one file ad-hoc, make env’s parent package namespace internal (non-exported) helpers resolve, source shared helpers : e <- new.env(parent = asNamespace("Rceattle")); (f list.files("tests/testthat","^helper",full.names=TRUE)) sys.source(f, e); testthat::test_file(f, env = e). plain new.env() makes tests fail spuriously find function "data_check". options(testthat.max_fails = Inf) shows failures. Tests run real fit_mod() optimization must use testthat::skip_on_cran() plain R CMD check / devtools::test() stay fast (NOT_CRAN=true runs ); leave fast unit tests unguarded. CI = .github/workflows/R-CMD-check.yaml (r-lib actions, multi-OS matrix) + pkgdown.yaml. lint config coverage gate. Slash commands wrap : /recompile, /test [file], /document, /check, /golden-check (defined .claude/commands/).
code: pkgload::load_all(".", quiet = TRUE)   # recompiles the TMB DLL + loads R/ (after any .cpp/.hpp edit) devtools::document(quiet = TRUE)       # regenerate man/*.Rd + NAMESPACE after roxygen changes NOT_CRAN=true Rscript -e 'devtools::test()'   # full suite (NOT_CRAN runs the skip_on_cran blocks) rcmdcheck::rcmdcheck()                 # what CI runs (slow; usually backgrounded)

title: Rceattle — Claude Code guide
text: R/ — numbered pipeline/collation order: 0-* build/prep helpers, 1-* data checks, 2..5-* params/map/bounds/rearrange, 6-* fit + rename output, 7-* plotting, 8-* sim, 9-* retro/jitter, 10-* MSE, 11-* model averaging. numeric prefixes meaningful — don’t renumber rename wholesale. src/TMB/ — ceattle_v01_11.cpp main model (~3,810 lines, numbered section index); process logic lives headers (recruitment.hpp, selectivity.hpp, predation.hpp, growth.hpp, linkage.hpp, comp_osa.hpp, helper_functions.hpp, bioenergetics.hpp, diet_data.hpp). tests/testthat/ — flat layout: every test top-level test-<area>-<topic>.R (e.g. test-selectivity-logisticpm.R, test-likelihood-index-covariance.R); old tests-Dynamics/ / tests-Selectivity/ … subdirectories removed. Shared helpers-*.R / fixtures/ sit alongside. Fast fixtures: make_test_data() (single-species) make_msm_test_data() (multispecies, incl. diet) estimateMode = 3 build non-optimized object. tests/comparison/ holds WHAM cross-checks (part test_check). vignettes/ eval = FALSE (need render). data/ bundled example datasets (BS2017SS, BS2017MS, GOA2018SS, …).

title: Rceattle — Claude Code guide
text: Commits: plain messages, AI-attribution / Co-Authored-trailer. Roxygen uses markdown; run devtools::document() touching @-docs. Trap: repo documented roxygen2 7.3.3 (DESCRIPTION: RoxygenNote: 7.3.3), newer local roxygen2 (e.g. 8.0.0) rewrites every man/*.Rd swaps RoxygenNote: Config/roxygen2/version: — huge spurious diff. document(), git checkout unrelated man/ + DESCRIPTION churn keep .Rd meant change. Give internal helpers @noRd (just @keywords internal) generate .Rd. Second trap: never insert helper function’s roxygen block definition. Contiguous #' lines ONE block bind whichever object follows, helper silently steals @export / @importFrom tags original function loses . Tests won’t catch (NAMESPACE isn’t regenerated) — next document() reveals . Put helpers block function. Released package — preserve public API. Rceattle shipped (v4.7.0, users; see cran-comments.md / inst/RELEASE-CHECKLIST.md). Exported build_*() args carry deprecation paths (e.g. SRR codes 1/3/5) — deprecate / keep back-compat rather deleting public surface. Internal refactors free long golden-reference equivalence holds. Match surrounding style. Canonical references: src/TMB/recruitment.hpp (Doxygen-documented header emulate) R/*.R + tests/testthat/* pair. codebase favors explanatory section headers Doxygen C++ — match local comment density; don’t strip comments. jnll_comp likelihood rows magic integers ceattle_v01_11.cpp; names live separately R/6-rename_output.R (~L130–151) kept sync hand. add/reorder likelihood component, update . Fleets sharing Selectivity_index / Q_index share ONE parameter block. adjust_map_shared_params() copies donor fleet’s map slice rest group, per-fleet setting differs within group silently taken donor (Sel_start_year, Bin_first_selected, N_sel_bins, …). donor first estimated fleet — fleet’s slice NA must never lead. Penalties priors shared block accumulated , lead fleet (flt_sel_lead / flt_q_lead); without gate counted per sharing fleet. GOA2018SS worked example (fleets 1 & 7 share selectivity; 9 & 10 share selectivity q). fleet_control$Fleet_code must equal row number. Per-fleet parameter map arrays dimensioned nrow(fleet_control) indexed Fleet_code, mismatch attaches parameters wrong fleet. data_check() enforces ; read fleet_control columns row index , never flt. Selectivity bin columns dimension-aware. Bin_first_selected, N_sel_bins, Sel_norm_bin1/2, Sel_pen_first_bin, Sel_pen_last_bin, Sel_cap_bin bin indices fleet’s Selectivity_dimension: absolute age age-based fleets (offset minage) 1-based length-bin ordinal length-based (offset 1). cpp penalties loop nbins, nages. new data_list element needs write_data() / read_data() support , round-trips nothing feature silently lossy standard xlsx format — index_cov lost. slow fit model, regression. full BS2017SS estimateMode = 0, phase = TRUE fit ~55 s: ~14 s one optimization, ~3x phasing, +~14 s sdreport. single fit needed ~500–700 nlminb iterations since least 2023 (bisected back main), don’t hunt recent cause. dev loops phase = FALSE, getsd = FALSE gives ~14 s. Numeric changes need golden-reference equivalence: edit can move fit must keep example fit (e.g. BS2017SS) within tolerance suite green. fit_mod(estimateMode=): 0 = hindcast + HCR projection, 1 = hindcast , 2 = projection-inits, 3 = build (MakeADFun) without optimizing, 4 = optimize params mapped . Mode 3 returns real objective, obj$fn() / obj$gr() usable diagnosing model fitting — analogue WHAM’s fit_wham(.fit = FALSE) SAM’s sam.fit(run = FALSE). (v4.7.1 mode 3 shared mode 4’s placeholder returned identically-zero gradient.) Mode 4 still returns placeholder jnll = dummy*dummy — build_map() maps every hindcast parameter , dummy free parameter objective plumbing smoke test, likelihood. Don’t read anything mode-4 objective, gradient, Hessian. fit_control() bundles optimizer / uncertainty knobs (getsd, bias.correct, loopnum, newtonsteps, getJointPrecision). Pass getsd = FALSE fast dev/test fits (skips sdreport) — sdrep NULL, vcov() returns NULL uncertainty bands NA. Scratch outputs (Rplots.pdf, *_osa.png, *.RDS tests/comparison/) gitignored — don’t commit .

what: Domain vocabulary (use these exact terms in plots/docs/messages)
title: Rceattle — Claude Code guide
text: Rceattle implements fisheries stock assessments — match vocabulary axis labels, documentation, console messages; don’t substitute lay phrasing. Reference points: Amendment-56 SPR proxies — F40% = max FABC, F35% = FOFL, B40% = BMSY proxy (Tier 3); Tier 1 uses estimated FMSY/BMSY. Don’t write “MSY” SPR proxy meant. SSB = female spawning-stock biomass; “recruitment deviations” (log-scale), “recruitment error”. Selectivity: name form (logistic / double-normal / gamma / nonparametric / semi-parametric) — don’t call every dome shape “double-normal”. Composition: age comps, length comps, conditional age--length (CAAL). ageing-error matrix applies age/CAAL data fit — length-stocks none. Data weighting: Francis (2011) McAllister–Ianelli Dirichlet-Multinomial. Diagnostics: Mohn’s rho (retrospective), OSA residuals, likelihood profiles.

text: following fields optional needed particular feature turned . title: 6. Building a data object in R
code: library(Rceattle)  # Define core dimensions up front — these drive the size of all downstream arrays. nspp     <- 2   # number of species (or stocks) nages    <- 10  # maximum age classes (same for all species here) nlengths <- 20  # number of length bins (for age-length keys / CAAL data) nyrs     <- 30  # number of hindcast years years    <- 1:nyrs  simData <- list()

title: 6. Building a data object in R
text: scalars vectors describe biological structure species control population model used.
code: simData$nspp    <- nspp simData$styr    <- 1       # first year of hindcast simData$endyr   <- nyrs    # last year of hindcast simData$projyr  <- nyrs + 10  # last year of the projection period  # Character labels shown in plots and output tables simData$spnames <- paste0("Species", 1:nspp)  # nsex: 1 = combined-sex model (male and female treated as one group), #        2 = sex-structured model (separate selectivity and mortality by sex) simData$nsex    <- rep(1, nspp)  # Calendar month of spawning — used to compute the fraction-of-year weight # applied to spawning stock biomass (e.g., 6 = mid-year spawning) simData$spawn_month <- rep(6, nspp)  simData$nages   <- rep(nages, nspp)   # number of age classes per species simData$minage  <- rep(1, nspp)       # minimum age (usually 1) simData$nlengths <- rep(nlengths, nspp)  # estDynamics controls how population abundance is estimated: #   0 = estimate population dynamics (standard statistical catch-at-age) #   1 = fix N-at-age exactly to values in NByageFixed (e.g., external estimates) #   2 = scale NByageFixed by a single estimated scalar per species simData$estDynamics <- rep(0, nspp)  # Indices linking each species to its weight and growth datasets. # Multiple weight schedules can exist (e.g., fleet-specific); these point to # which one is used for total biomass (pop) and spawning biomass (ssb). simData$pop_wt_index <- 1:nspp simData$ssb_wt_index <- 1:nspp simData$pop_age_transition_index <- rep(1, nspp)  # Length-weight relationship coefficients: W = alpha * L ^ beta. # Used internally to convert length-based selectivity to weight when estimating growth. simData$alpha_wt_len <- rep(0.00001, nspp) simData$beta_wt_len  <- rep(3, nspp)  # Prior or initial standard deviation for log-recruitment deviations. Controls the # strength of the recruitment penalty in penalized-likelihood mode. simData$sigma_rec_prior <- rep(1, nspp)  # Non-modelled ("other") prey biomass available to predators. Used in # multi-species mode to prevent unrealistically high predation mortality when # modelled prey are scarce. Setting this too low forces predators to over-eat # modelled prey; too high dilutes the predation signal. simData$other_food <- rep(1e5, nspp)

title: 6. Building a data object in R
text: important configuration table. row defines one fleet (fishery survey) controls modelled. Multiple fleets can target species.
code: # Fleet_type: #   "Fishery" -- contributes catch and catch-at-age/length composition data #   "Survey"  -- contributes an abundance index and composition data #   "Off"     -- fleet is present in the data but excluded from the likelihood  # Selectivity options (Selectivity column) — use the string name or integer code: #   "Fixed"              (0) -- fixed at values in emp_sel; not estimated #   "Logistic"           (1) -- two-parameter ascending logistic (a50, slope) #   "NonParametric"      (2) -- freely estimated selectivity-at-age/length with smoothness penalty #   "DoubleLogistic"     (3) -- ascending + descending dome-shaped logistic #   "DescendingLogistic" (4) -- descending logistic only (dome-shaped for oldest ages) #   "Hake"               (5) -- non-parametric selectivity à la Taylor et al. (Pacific hake) #   "2DAR1"              (6) -- 2D autoregressive random effects (age × year) #   "3DAR1"              (7) -- 3D autoregressive random effects (age × year × cohort) # # Selectivity_dimension: "Age" or "Length" #   Length-based selectivity requires an age-to-length transition matrix (see below).  # Catchability options (Catchability column) — use the string name or integer code: #   "Fixed"                (0) -- Q fixed at Q_prior; not estimated #   "Estimated"            (1) -- freely estimated on log scale #   "Estimated-with-prior" (2) -- estimated with a lognormal prior (Q_prior, Q_sd_prior) #   "Analytical"           (3) -- Ludwig & Walters / Martell (1994) analytical Q #   "PowerEquation"        (4) -- power-equation Q (habitat area scaling) #   "Environmental"        (5) -- mu_q + X * beta, where X is a covariate in env_data #   "AR1"                  (6) -- auto-regressive catchability (Rogers et al. 2024) #   NA                         -- not applicable (use for fisheries without CPUE)  # Comp_loglike / CAAL_loglike options: #   "Multinomial"           -- standard multinomial #   "DirichletMultinomial"  -- overdispersed; estimates a concentration parameter #   "MultinomialAFSC"       -- AFSC variant of multinomial (marginal age + length)  simData$fleet_control <- data.frame(   Fleet_name  = paste0(c("Survey", "Fishery"),                        rep(paste(" Species", 1:nspp), each = 2)),   Fleet_code  = 1:(nspp * 2),       # unique integer ID per fleet   Fleet_type  = rep(c("Survey", "Fishery"), nspp),   Species     = rep(1:nspp, each = 2),   Month       = 0,                   # 0 = mid-year; calendar month otherwise    # Selectivity_index links fleets that share the same selectivity curve.   # Fleets with the same index share all selectivity parameters.   Selectivity_index         = 1:(nspp * 2),   Selectivity               = "Logistic",   Selectivity_dimension     = "Age",   N_sel_bins                = NA,    # used for NonParametric only   Sel_curve_pen1            = NA,    # smoothness penalty (NonParametric)   Sel_curve_pen2            = NA,   # Time_varying_sel:   #   0 / "Off" = time-invariant (default)   #   1 / "IID" = penalized log-normal deviates (SD fixed at Time_varying_sel_sd_prior   #       unless random_sel = TRUE in fit_mod)   #   2 / "AR1" = AR(1) (not yet implemented)   #   3 / "Block" = time blocks (specify via R-side mapping)   #   4 / "RandomWalk" = random walk   #   5 / "RandomWalkAscending" = random walk on ascending portion of double logistic   Time_varying_sel          = 0,   Time_varying_sel_sd_prior = 1,   Bin_first_selected        = 1,     # youngest fully-selected age or length bin   Sel_norm_bin1             = NA,    # bin to normalise selectivity from (optional)   Sel_norm_bin2             = NA,    # Composition likelihoods   Comp_loglike = "Multinomial",   Comp_weights = 1,                  # input effective sample size multiplier   CAAL_loglike = "Multinomial",   CAAL_weights = 1,    # Index units and weight/growth linkage   Weight1_Numbers2     = 1,          # 1 = weight (mt), 2 = numbers   Weight_index         = rep(1:nspp, each = 2),   Age_transition_index = 1,    # Q_index links fleets that share the same catchability parameter.   Q_index              = 1:(nspp * 2),   Catchability         = rep(c("Estimated", NA), nspp),   Q_prior              = rep(c(1,   NA), nspp),   Q_sd_prior           = rep(c(0.2, NA), nspp),   # Time_varying_q:   #   0 / "Off" = time-invariant   #   1 / "IID" = penalized log-normal deviates (SD fixed at Time_varying_q_sd_prior   #       unless random_q = TRUE in fit_mod)   #   2 / "AR1" = AR(1) (not yet implemented)   #   3 / "Block" = time blocks   #   4 / "RandomWalk" = random walk   Time_varying_q          = rep(c(0, NA), nspp),   Time_varying_q_sd_prior = rep(c(1, NA), nspp),    # Estimate_index_sd:   #   0 = fix at Log_sd from index_data   #   1 = estimate a single SD   #   2 = analytical sigma (Ludwig & Walters 1994)   Estimate_index_sd  = rep(c(0,  NA), nspp),   Index_sd_prior     = rep(c(1,  NA), nspp),    # Estimate_catch_sd:   #   0 = fix at Log_sd from catch_data (treats catch as known)   #   1 = estimate   Estimate_catch_sd  = rep(c(NA, 0),  nspp),   Catch_sd_prior     = rep(c(NA, 1),  nspp),    # proj_F_prop: how future F is distributed across fishery fleets per species.   # Must sum to 1 across fishery fleets for each species. NA for surveys.   proj_F_prop = rep(c(NA, 1), nspp) )

title: 6. Building a data object in R
text: One row per fleet-year combination survey fleets. Observation log-scale biomass index (numbers Weight1_Numbers2 = 2). negative Year value tells Rceattle predict index without including likelihood, useful model checking.
code: simData$index_data <- data.frame(   Fleet_name        = rep(paste("Survey Species", 1:nspp), each = nyrs),   Fleet_code        = rep(seq(1, nspp * 2, by = 2), each = nyrs),   Species           = rep(1:nspp, each = nyrs),   Year              = rep(years, nspp),   Month             = 0,   # Selectivity_block: integer index into the selectivity/Q parameter block.   # Used when Time_varying_sel or Time_varying_q = 3 (time blocks).   Selectivity_block = 1,   Observation       = rnorm(nyrs * nspp),   # replace with real log-index values   Log_sd            = 0.1                   # observation SE on the log scale )

title: 6. Building a data object in R
text: One row per fishery fleet-year combination. Log_sd typically set small (0.01–0.05) catch treated known; increase catch highly uncertain.
code: simData$catch_data <- data.frame(   Fleet_name        = rep(paste("Fishery Species", 1:nspp), each = nyrs),   Fleet_code        = rep(seq(2, nspp * 2, by = 2), each = nyrs),   Species           = rep(1:nspp, each = nyrs),   Year              = rep(years, nspp),   Month             = 0,   Selectivity_block = 1,   Catch             = abs(rnorm(nyrs * nspp)),  # replace with real catch (mt)   Log_sd            = 0.05 )

title: 6. Building a data object in R
text: Age length composition data. Age0_Length1 = 0 age compositions, 1 length compositions. Sex = 0 combined sex, 1 females, 2 males, 3 joint female+male. Composition columns (Comp_1, Comp_2, …) can raw counts proportions — Rceattle normalises internally. Skip section entirely (don’t set simData$comp_data) composition data available — clean_data() fill empty data.frame.
code: comp_matrix <- matrix(abs(rnorm(nyrs * nspp * nages * 2)),                       nrow = nyrs * nspp * 2, ncol = nages) colnames(comp_matrix) <- paste0("Comp_", 1:nages)  simData$comp_data <- cbind(   data.frame(     Fleet_name   = c(rep(paste("Survey Species",  1:nspp), each = nyrs),                      rep(paste("Fishery Species", 1:nspp), each = nyrs)),     Fleet_code   = rep(c(seq(1, nspp * 2, 2), seq(2, nspp * 2, 2)), each = nyrs),     Species      = c(rep(1:nspp, each = nyrs), rep(1:nspp, each = nyrs)),     Sex          = 0,     Age0_Length1 = 0,     Year         = rep(years, 2 * nspp),     Month        = 0,     Sample_size  = 200   ),   comp_matrix )

title: 6. Building a data object in R
text: CAAL data provide observed age frequencies within length bin allow model jointly fit length age compositions, optionally estimate growth curve internally (see vignette("model-parameterizations") ?build_growth). One row per fleet-sex-year-length-bin combination. caal_data becomes required growth estimated internally ((growth_model > 0)); otherwise can omitted.
code: caal_matrix <- matrix(abs(rnorm(nyrs * nspp * nages * 2 * nlengths)),                       nrow = nyrs * nspp * 2 * nlengths, ncol = nages) colnames(caal_matrix) <- paste0("CAAL_", 1:nages)  simData$caal_data <- cbind(   data.frame(     Fleet_name  = c(rep(paste("Survey Species",  1:nspp), each = nyrs * nlengths),                     rep(paste("Fishery Species", 1:nspp), each = nyrs * nlengths)),     Fleet_code  = rep(c(seq(1, nspp * 2, 2), seq(2, nspp * 2, 2)),                       each = nyrs * nlengths),     Species     = c(rep(1:nspp, each = nyrs * nlengths),                     rep(1:nspp, each = nyrs * nlengths)),     Sex         = 0,     Year        = rep(years, 2 * nspp * nlengths),     Length      = rep(1:nlengths, 2 * nspp * nyrs),     Sample_size = 200   ),   caal_matrix )

title: 6. Building a data object in R
text: probability fish age observed length bin l. Required fitting length compositions estimating growth internally. row must sum 1. placeholder uses identity matrix (age maps exactly length bin ); replace empirical model-based growth matrices.
code: age_trans_list <- lapply(1:nspp, function(sp) {   tmp <- matrix(0, nrow = nages, ncol = nlengths)   diag(tmp[1:min(nages, nlengths), 1:min(nages, nlengths)]) <- 1   colnames(tmp) <- paste0("Length_", 1:nlengths)   cbind(data.frame(Age_transition_name  = paste("Species", sp),                    Age_transition_index = sp,                    Species              = sp,                    Sex                  = 0,                    Age                  = 1:nages), tmp) }) simData$age_trans_matrix <- do.call(rbind, age_trans_list)

title: 6. Building a data object in R
text: probability fish true age t read observed age o. identity matrix (error) conservative starting point. Ageing error matrices can generated standard tools (e.g., AgeingError package) substituted .
code: age_error_list <- lapply(1:nspp, function(sp) {   tmp <- as.data.frame(diag(1, nages))   colnames(tmp) <- paste0("Obs_age", 1:nages)   cbind(data.frame(Species = sp, True_age = 1:nages), tmp) }) simData$age_error <- do.call(rbind, age_error_list)

title: 6. Building a data object in R
text: Mean weight (kg) age. Setting Year = 0 applies schedule years (time-invariant). Providing multiple rows different years enables time-varying weight--age, used empirical weight--age models.
code: weight_matrix <- matrix((1:nages / nages)^3 * 0.01,                         nrow = nspp, ncol = nages, byrow = TRUE) colnames(weight_matrix) <- paste0("Age", 1:nages)  simData$weight <- cbind(   data.frame(Wt_name  = paste("Species", 1:nspp),              Wt_index = 1:nspp,              Species  = 1:nspp,              Sex      = 0,              Year     = 0),   # Year = 0 → time-invariant   weight_matrix )

title: 6. Building a data object in R
text: Proportion mature age, used compute spawning stock biomass. Values range 0 1. sex-structured models (nsex = 2) represents proportion females mature.
code: mat_matrix <- matrix(1, nrow = nspp, ncol = nages) colnames(mat_matrix) <- paste0("Age", 1:nages) simData$maturity <- cbind(data.frame(Species = 1:nspp), mat_matrix)

title: 6. Building a data object in R
text: Proportion female age. Used combined-sex models (nsex = 1) weight spawning biomass contributions. two-sex models (nsex = 2) proportion female recruitment.
code: sex_matrix <- matrix(0.5, nrow = nspp, ncol = nages) colnames(sex_matrix) <- paste0("Age", 1:nages) simData$sex_ratio <- cbind(data.frame(Species = 1:nspp), sex_matrix)

title: 6. Building a data object in R
text: Pre-specified selectivity--age values fleets whose selectivity fixed (estimated). Required fleet Selectivity = "Fixed". Skip fleets estimate selectivity (example). need , table looks like:
code: # Example for one fleet whose selectivity is fixed at the supplied row of values emp_sel <- data.frame(   Fleet_name = "Survey Species 1",   Fleet_code = 1,   Species    = 1,   Sex        = 0,   Year       = 0,                       # 0 = applied to every year   t(matrix(c(0.1, 0.5, 1, rep(1, nages - 3)), ncol = 1,            dimnames = list(paste0("Comp_", 1:nages), NULL))) ) simData$emp_sel <- NULL

title: 6. Building a data object in R
text: Used estDynamics > 0: 1 = numbers--age fixed exactly values 2 = numbers--age scaled single estimated scalar per species 3 = numbers--age scaled age-specific estimated scalars per species Required (estDynamics > 0). Skip ’re estimating population dynamics scratch (default estDynamics = 0). need , table columns Species_name, Species, Sex, Year, Age1 ... Age<nages> fixed numbers--age.

title: 6. Building a data object in R
text: Residual natural mortality--age predation component. single-species mode, total mortality M = M1. multi-species mode, M = M1 + M2 M2 predation mortality estimated bioenergetics model. switching multi-species mode important reduce M1 accordingly (see vignette("single-vs-multispecies")). M1 can also estimated rather fixed. See ?build_M1 options including estimating single scalar, age-specific vector, temperature-dependent function.
code: m_matrix <- matrix(0.2, nrow = nspp, ncol = nages) colnames(m_matrix) <- paste0("Age", 1:nages) simData$M1_base <- cbind(data.frame(Species = 1:nspp, Sex = 0), m_matrix)

title: 6. Building a data object in R
text: optional time series used environment-recruitment, -M1, -catchability, -growth relationships. Missing years filled column mean. Column names Year can anything referenced column order. Skip environmental covariates used. clean_data() fall back Year-data.frame indices, data_check() complain feature actually needs index (env-q catchability, Ceq[sp] > 1, env linkage).
code: simData$env_data <- data.frame(   Year    = 1:nyrs,   EnvData = 1       # constant = no environmental effect (placeholder) )

what: 8. Multi-species bioenergetics parameters (optional in single-species mode)
title: 6. Building a data object in R
text: parameters govern Wisconsin bioenergetics model used compute predation mortality (M2) multi-species mode. unused single-species mode can omitted entirely — Rceattle fills missing scalars safe defaults. multi-species mode (msmMode > 0) Ceq, Cindex, Pvalue, fday, CA, CB, Qc, Tco, Tcm, Tcl, CK1, CK4 must supplied length-nspp vectors; data_check() list missing wrong-length. Likewise diet_data ration_data required. See ?build_M1 CEATTLE technical documentation full details parameter.
code: # Ceq: consumption (bioenergetics) equation form for each species: #   1 = Exponential (Stewart et al. 1983) #   2 = Warm-water temperature dependence (Kitchell et al. 1977) #   3 = Cool/cold-water temperature dependence (Thornton & Lessem 1979) #   4 = bypass bioenergetics; use ration_data directly (set CA = 1, fday = 1, CB = 0) simData$Ceq    <- rep(4,  nspp)  simData$Cindex <- rep(1,  nspp)   # temperature index type simData$Pvalue <- rep(1,  nspp)   # proportion of maximum consumption realised simData$fday   <- rep(1,  nspp)   # foraging days per year  # Wisconsin model coefficients (CA, CB) and temperature dependence parameters simData$CA  <- rep(1,  nspp) simData$CB  <- rep(-1, nspp) simData$Qc  <- rep(1,  nspp) simData$Tco <- rep(1,  nspp) simData$Tcm <- rep(1,  nspp) simData$Tcl <- rep(1,  nspp) simData$CK1 <- rep(1,  nspp) simData$CK4 <- rep(1,  nspp)  # Diet composition likelihood for each predator species # 0 = Multinomial, 1 = Dirichlet-multinomial simData$Diet_loglike      <- rep(0, nspp) simData$Diet_comp_weights <- rep(1, nspp)  # Ration data (optional in single-species mode): observed mean ration-at-age from # bioenergetics studies. Required when msmMode > 0. Skip in single-species mode. # # When provided, columns are: Species, Sex, Year, Age1, ..., Age<nages>.  # Diet composition data: observed stomach content proportions (predator-prey pairs). # Required when msmMode > 0; skip in single-species mode. # # When provided, columns are: Pred, Prey, Pred_sex, Prey_sex, Pred_age, # Prey_age, Year, Sample_size, Stomach_proportion_by_weight.

code: plot_data(simData) # Key fit_mod() arguments: # # estimateMode: 0 = full fit (hindcast + projection) #               1 = hindcast only #               2 = projection only (fix parameters, run HCR) #               3 = evaluate only (MakeADFun, no optimisation) -- useful for debugging # # msmMode:      0 = single-species, 1 = Type II MSVPA, 2 = Type III MSVPA # # initMode:     0 = freely estimated initial N-at-age #               1 = equilibrium, F_init = 0, no init deviations #               2 = equilibrium, F_init = 0, with init deviations (default) #               3 = non-equilibrium: F_init estimated, init devs included #               4 = non-equilibrium: F_init scales R0 # # phase:        TRUE = use parameter phasing for improved convergence (recommended)  sim_run <- fit_mod(   data_list    = simData,   estimateMode = 3,    # change to 0 for a real fit   msmMode      = 0,   initMode     = 2,   random_rec   = FALSE,   fit_control = fit_control(     phase        = TRUE,     verbose      = 1))

title: Environmental linkages and priors: a formula-driven API
text: Environmental drivers (temperature, prey density, climate indices) enter stock assessments recruitment, natural mortality, growth, catchability, selectivity. Rceattle exposes long-format linkage table: one row per estimated coefficient tying environmental term (user-specified design column) process parameter. Users describe linkages linkage_spec() – formula-driven helper – pass result relevant build_*() function. fit_mod() pools every spec single data.frame paired shared design matrix; TMB template iterates table adds per-process offsets underlying linear predictors. linkage path wired growth (von Bertalanffy Richards), natural mortality (M1), recruitment (R0, alpha, beta).

what: A first example: temperature on K
title: Environmental linkages and priors: a formula-driven API
text: Suppose want sex- species-specific von Bertalanffy growth, von Bertalanffy K parameter responding temperature index species:
code: library(Rceattle) data(whamGrowthData) plot_data(whamGrowthData)  # Use logistic selectivity for all fleets in this example. whamGrowthData$fleet_control$Selectivity <- "Logistic" whamGrowthData$fleet_control$Selectivity_dimension <- "Length"  # 1. Attach an env_data table to the data list. Must include `Year` #    plus whatever covariates show up in your formulas. Here `temp` is #    a placeholder; in real use it would be a standardised SST series, #    PDO index, etc. yrs <- whamGrowthData$styr:whamGrowthData$endyr whamGrowthData$env_data <- data.frame(   Year = yrs,   temp = rnorm(length(yrs), 0, 0.1) )  # 2. Build a growth specification with one linkage per parameter that #    you want to vary. linkage_spec() captures (formula, by, link, #    init, bounds, priors) for one process parameter. growth_spec <- build_growth(   fun = "vonBertalanffy",   linkages = list(     K = linkage_spec(       formula = ~ temp,             # 2 columns: (Intercept) and `temp`       by      = ~ species + sex,    # one beta per (species, sex, column)       priors  = list(temp = normal(0, 0.1)) # Tight prior     )   ) )  # 3. Fit as usual. fit <- fit_mod(   data_list   = whamGrowthData,   growthFun   = growth_spec,   estimateMode = 0,    msmMode     = 0,   fit_control = fit_control(verbose = 0) ) summary(fit)

title: Environmental linkages and priors: a formula-driven API
text: Key arguments (see ?linkage_spec full list): formula – one-sided R formula describing linear predictor (anything model.matrix() understands: ~ 1, ~ temp, ~ temp + PDO, ~ poly(temp, 2), factor predictors, etc.). param – target parameter name (e.g. "K"). Filled automatically spec registered linkages = list(K = ...) list key. – stratifying factors (default ~species); use ~species + sex per-(species, sex) coefficients, NULL share single coefficient set. species / sex – restrict spec specific ids. Use multi-spec form (Per-species / Per-sex formulas ) give different species sexes different formulas. sex accepts integers (1L, 2L) strings ("Females"/"Males", case-insensitive). link – relates linear predictor natural-scale target. "log" (default) gives multiplicative effect natural param; "identity" gives additive effect natural param. init / bounds – named lists keyed design-matrix column (init = list(temp = 0.05), bounds = list(temp = c(-2, 2))). priors – named list keyed design-matrix column. entry either Rceattle_prior list keyed species id; see Priors . re_group / est_phase – random-effects grouping (placeholder) estimation phase ordinal (0 fixes, 1+ estimates).
code: linkage_spec(   formula,   param     = NULL,   by        = ~ species,   species   = NULL,   sex       = NULL,   link      = "log",                # or "identity"   init      = NULL,   bounds    = NULL,   priors    = NULL,   re_group  = NA_character_,   est_phase = 1L )

title: Environmental linkages and priors: a formula-driven API
text: Four families available, plus implicit “none”: Inside linkage_spec(priors = ...) unprefixed shorthand normal(), lognormal(), gamma(), beta() resolves corresponding prior_* constructors via private data mask – scoped priors argument mask base::gamma() / base::beta() elsewhere: Prior semantics. (Intercept) rows, Priors evaluated natural-scale (e.g. normal(0.3, 0.1) K means dnorm(K_natural, 0.3, 0.1)). Use lognormal(meanlog, sdlog) put normal directly log scale. covariate rows, prior applies coefficient -regardless link function. programmatic prior assembly (e.g. species-specific priors built loop) call prior_* constructors directly: prior’s negative log-density contributes Linkage-table priors row joint NLL:
code: prior_normal(mean, sd) prior_lognormal(meanlog, sdlog) prior_gamma(shape, rate) prior_beta(shape1, shape2) linkage_spec(   formula = ~ temp + PDO,   by      = ~ species,   priors  = list(     temp = normal(0, 1),     # informative, ~95% in (-2, 2)     PDO  = normal(0, 5)      # weak   ) ) priors <- lapply(species_specific_sds, function(s) prior_normal(0, s)) names(priors) <- c("temp", "PDO", "salinity") linkage_spec(formula = ~ temp + PDO + salinity, priors = priors) fit$quantities$jnll_comp["Linkage-table priors", ]

what: Putting a prior on the parameter itself
title: Environmental linkages and priors: a formula-driven API
text: Bayesian-style informative priors can applied directly base growth parameters (K, L1, Linf, m), natural mortality (M1), recruitment parameters (R0, alpha, beta). prior attached (Intercept) row re-targeted base parameter. syntax used column. pattern works linkage target – Linf, L1, m (Richards), M1, R0, alpha, beta.
code: # Example: prior on K for von Bertalanffy growth growth_spec <- build_growth(   fun = "vonBertalanffy",   linkages = list(     K = linkage_spec(       formula = ~ 1,                              # intercept only -- no env effects       by      = ~ species + sex,       init    = list(`(Intercept)` = 0.3),   # start at K = 0.3       # Use `lognormal(log(0.3), 0.1)` to get a normal prior on log(K).       priors  = list(`(Intercept)` = lognormal(log(0.3), 0.1))     )   ) )

title: Environmental linkages and priors: a formula-driven API
text: standard deviations length--age L1 Linf anchors (sd_L1, sd_Linf) exposed linkage targets , init / bounds / priors contract applies. route onto growth_log_sd parameter rather log_growth_pars, – growth_log_sd year dimension growth.hpp – intercept-bearing formulas honored. Slope rows targets raise warning effect; slope-formulas (~ 0 + temp) error. can also key prior species id species- specific priors: prior contribution appears slot 20 joint NLL: can inspect linked parameter values via linkage table, estimated slope coefficients, base-parameter array: approach works M1 want prior natural mortality : linkage prior applied verbatim, lognormal bias-correction term.
code: # Prior on the SD at L1 anchored at exp(log(5)) = 5 length units, # with a tight normal prior on the log scale. growth_spec_sd <- build_growth(   fun = "vonBertalanffy",   linkages = list(     sd_L1   = linkage_spec(       formula = ~ 1,       by      = ~ species + sex,       init    = list(`(Intercept)` = 5),       # Prior on log-scale SD; switch to `normal(5, 0.3)`       # for a Normal on sd_L1.       priors  = list(`(Intercept)` = lognormal(log(5), 0.3))     ),     sd_Linf = linkage_spec(       formula = ~ 1,       by      = ~ species + sex,       init    = list(`(Intercept)` = 15)     )   ) )  # After fit_mod(), the init values land on growth_log_sd[, , 1:2] # (SD at L1 and SD at Linf, log-scale), and the priors evaluate # against those base-parameter cells via the intercept re-targeting # path described above. rec_spec <- build_srr(   srr_fun = 0,   linkages = list(     R0 = linkage_spec(       formula = ~ 1,       by      = ~ species,       init    = list(`(Intercept)` = 1000),       # Species-keyed priors on log-scale R0.       priors  = list(`(Intercept)` = list(         `1` = lognormal(log(1000), 0.2),         `2` = lognormal(log(1500), 0.3),         `3` = lognormal(log(800),  0.25)       ))     )   ) ) fit$quantities$jnll_comp["Linkage-table priors", ] fit$data_list$linkage_table[fit$data_list$linkage_table$param == "K", ] fit$estimated_params$beta_linkage          # (Intercept) rows are 0; slopes are estimated fit$estimated_params$log_growth_pars       # base K / L1 / Linf / m (on log scale internally) data("GOApollock") # Using GOA pollock as an example  # One-species model, lognormal(log(0.34), 0.01) prior on M1 # applied via the linkage intercept (equivalent to a Normal on log_M1). # The structural M1_model is kept at "sex_age_invariant" (= 1). M1_spec <- build_M1(   M1_model = "sex_age_invariant",   linkages = list(     M1 = linkage_spec(       formula = ~ 1,       by      = ~ species,       init    = list(`(Intercept)` = 0.34),       # Prior is on the natural-scale for M1.       # `lognormal(log(0.34), 0.01)` evaluates Normal on log(M1).       # Use `normal(0.34, 0.01)` for a Normal directly on natural M1.       priors  = list(`(Intercept)` = lognormal(log(0.34), 0.01))     )   ) )  # Fit the model - no manual mapping needed fit <- fit_mod(   data_list = GOApollock,   M1Fun     = M1_spec,   estimateMode = 0,   fit_control = fit_control(phase = TRUE) )

title: Environmental linkages and priors: a formula-driven API
text: entry priors = list(...) may : single prior – applies every species/sex row uses design column, named list priors keyed species id – one prior per specified species, named list priors keyed species id sex – one prior per specified species sex, two-level nested list keyed first specified species, specified sex id. sexually dimorphic stocks, temp column can take different priors per (species, sex). level value can either Rceattle_prior (applies sub-strata) list drills : syntax works prior family. recommended pattern covariate different prior strength across stocks (e.g. one species prior literature temp sensitivity another doesn’t), within species sexes expected respond differently. Built programmatically, ’s just:
code: # Species-only keying linkage_spec(   formula = ~ temp,   by      = ~ species,   priors  = list(     temp = list(       `1` = normal(0, 0.1),    # tight prior for species 1       #`2` = normal(0, 0.5),   # No prior species 2       `3` = normal(0, 1.0)     # weakest for species 3       # any species not listed gets no prior     )   ) ) linkage_spec(   formula = ~ temp,   by      = ~ species + sex,   priors  = list(     temp = list(       # Species 1: different tightness per sex.       `1` = list(`1` = normal(0, 0.1),    # sp 1, sex 1 (e.g. females)                  `2` = normal(0, 0.2)),   # sp 1, sex 2 (e.g. males)       # Species 2: scalar applies to every sex.       `2` = normal(0, 0.5)       # Any (species, sex) combination not listed gets no prior.     )   ) ) sd_by_species <- c(`1` = 0.1, `2` = 0.5, `3` = 1.0) priors_per_sp <- lapply(sd_by_species, function(s) prior_normal(0, s))  linkage_spec(   formula = ~ temp,   by      = ~ species,   priors  = list(temp = priors_per_sp) )

M1_spec <- build_M1(   M1_model = "sex_specific",   linkages = list(     M1 = list(       linkage_spec(         formula = ~ 1,         by      = ~ species + sex,         sex     = "Females",                              # or sex = 1L         init    = list(`(Intercept)` = 0.12),         priors  = list(`(Intercept)` = lognormal(log(0.12), 0.0001))       ),       linkage_spec(         formula = ~ 1,         by      = ~ species + sex,         sex     = "Males",                                # or sex = 2L         init    = list(`(Intercept)` = 0.20),         priors  = list(`(Intercept)` = lognormal(log(0.20), 0.0001))       )     )   ) )

title: Environmental linkages and priors: a formula-driven API
text: formula passed linkage_spec() fed straight stats::model.matrix(), expression model.matrix() understands works – polynomial bases, splines, interactions, arithmetic transformations. Polynomials. Use poly() orthogonal polynomial bases (default; numerically well-conditioned), poly(..., raw = TRUE) raw monomials. basis order shows separate design column coefficient: poly() orthogonalises basis rows env_data, columns zero-mean model years linear slope, quadratic curvature, etc. estimated independently – generally right choice don’t specific scientific reason prefer raw monomials. Arbitrary arithmetic. Use () insert literal expression (otherwise temp^2 interpreted formula crossing operator reduces temp): design column name deparsed call ((temp^2)), key init, bounds, priors use string – backticks let write name. Splines. Natural cubic splines via splines::ns() work ---box often better choice high-order polynomials want flexibility without strong tail behaviour: Interactions. temp:PDO adds single product column; temp * PDO shorthand temp + PDO + temp:PDO: Mixing forms across species. Combined per-species formula machinery, can give one species polynomial response another linear one without duplicating columns: practical caution: -named columns must numerically identical across specs use . deterministic formulas evaluated env_data automatic; can fail ’ve built specs different env_data frames.
code: # 4th-order orthogonal polynomial in temp, by species. linkage_spec(   formula = ~ poly(temp, 4),   by      = ~ species ) # design columns produced: #   (Intercept), poly(temp, 4)1, poly(temp, 4)2, #   poly(temp, 4)3, poly(temp, 4)4 # Linear + raw quadratic in temp. linkage_spec(   formula = ~ temp + I(temp^2),   by      = ~ species,   priors  = list(`I(temp^2)` = normal(0, 0.1))   # tight prior on curvature ) linkage_spec(   formula = ~ splines::ns(temp, df = 4),   by      = ~ species ) linkage_spec(   formula = ~ temp * PDO,   by      = ~ species,   priors  = list(`temp:PDO` = normal(0, 0.5)) ) build_growth(   fun = "vonBertalanffy",   linkages = list(     K = list(       linkage_spec(formula = ~ poly(temp, 3),                    by = ~ species, species = 1L),       linkage_spec(formula = ~ temp,                    by = ~ species, species = 2L)     )   ) )

New code prefer linkages – composes naturally priors, bounds, per-species formulas. Inspecting result: Growth M linkages share table – one fit can carry linkage rows processes, underlying coefficient vector beta_linkage indexes .
code: yrs <- GOApollock$styr:GOApollock$endyr GOApollock$env_data <- data.frame(   Year = yrs,   temp = rnorm(length(yrs), 0, 0.1) )  M1_spec <- build_M1(   M1_model = "sex_age_invariant",            # or M1_model = 1 (back-compat)   linkages = list(     M1 = linkage_spec(       formula = ~ temp,       by      = ~ species,       priors  = list(temp = normal(0, 0.1))     )   ) )  fit <- fit_mod(   data_list   = GOApollock,   M1Fun       = M1_spec,   estimateMode = 0,   msmMode     = 0 ) build_M1(M1_model = "sex_age_specific", M1_re = "ar1_age")   # = 3, 4 build_M1(M1_model = 3,                  M1_re = 4)            # equivalent fit$data_list$linkage_table         # rows have process == "M" fit$quantities$M_linkage_offset     # [nspp, max_sex, max_age, nyrs] fit$quantities$jnll_comp["Linkage-table priors", ]

title: Environmental linkages and priors: a formula-driven API
text: build_srr() accepts linkages argument three allowed parameter keys: R0 – meaningful srr_fun; right target recruitment respond env without fitting SRR. alpha (productivity) beta (density-dependence) – work srr_fun %% c(2, 3, 4, 5) (Beverton-Holt Ricker). structural choice (srr_fun) accepts either integer codes readable strings interchangeably: Inspecting result: Practical note: linkage row’s age_bin ignored recruitment (recruitment age 0 definition). sex_ratio data input partitions recruits across sexes downstream.
code: # Mean-recruitment with a temperature linkage on R0. rec_spec <- build_srr(   srr_fun  = "mean",                       # = 0   linkages = list(     R0 = linkage_spec(       formula = ~ temp,       priors  = list(temp = normal(0, 0.5))     )   ) )  # Beverton-Holt with env effects on alpha (and species-keyed # priors so each stock has its own sensitivity). rec_spec_bh <- build_srr(   srr_fun  = "BevertonHolt",               # = 2   linkages = list(     alpha = linkage_spec(       formula = ~ temp,       priors  = list(         temp = list(`1` = normal(0, 0.3),                     `2` = normal(0, 0.7))       )     )   ) )  fit <- fit_mod(   data_list   = data_list,   recFun      = rec_spec,   estimateMode = 0,   msmMode     = 0 ) build_srr(srr_fun = "mean")           # = 0 build_srr(srr_fun = "BevertonHolt")   # = 2 build_srr(srr_fun = "Ricker")         # = 4 fit$data_list$linkage_table             # rows have process == "recruitment" fit$quantities$recruitment_linkage_offset  # [nspp, n_rec_params, nyrs]                                            # n_rec_params = 3 (R0, alpha, beta)

title: Environmental linkages and priors: a formula-driven API
text: pattern composes one parameter linked: pooler : compute one shared X = model.matrix(~ temp + PDO, env_data) three columns, emit 4 (sp × sex) + 3 (Linf cols) × 3 (sp) + 3 (m intercepts) = 16 rows linkage table, match -named columns ((Intercept), temp) across specs ’s duplication X. Per-process logic (vB m; Richards ) enforced build time: Growth, M, recruitment can linked fit – build_*() output carries linkages list fit_mod() pools single shared design matrix:
code: growth_spec <- build_growth(   fun = "Richards",   linkages = list(     K    = linkage_spec(       formula = ~ temp,       by      = ~ species + sex,       priors  = list(temp = normal(0, 1))     ),     Linf = linkage_spec(       formula = ~ temp + PDO,       by      = ~ species,       priors  = list(temp = normal(0, 0.5),                      PDO  = normal(0, 0.5))     ),     m    = linkage_spec(       formula = ~ 1,             # intercept only -- no env effect       by      = ~ species     )   ) ) build_growth(   fun = "vonBertalanffy",   linkages = list(m = linkage_spec(~ temp)) ) #> Error: linkages$m is only valid with fun = 'Richards'; ... fit <- fit_mod(   data_list   = data_list,   growthFun   = build_growth(     fun      = "vonBertalanffy",     linkages = list(       K = linkage_spec(formula = ~ temp)     )   ),   M1Fun       = build_M1(     M1_model = "sex_age_invariant",     linkages = list(       M1 = linkage_spec(formula = ~ temp)     )   ),   recFun      = build_srr(     srr_fun  = "mean",     linkages = list(       R0 = linkage_spec(formula = ~ temp)     )   ),   estimateMode = 0,   msmMode     = 0 )  # Linkage table contains rows for all three processes: table(fit$data_list$linkage_table$process) #>      growth           M  recruitment #>           4           4            4

Useful for verifying the linkage # fired as you intended. str(fit$quantities$growth_linkage_offset) str(fit$quantities$M_linkage_offset) str(fit$quantities$recruitment_linkage_offset)  # Per-row coefficient values in the same order as `linkage_table`. fit$estimated_params$beta_linkage  # The prior NLL contribution from slot 19 of jnll_comp. fit$quantities$jnll_comp["Linkage-table priors", ]

what: Behind the scenes: automatic base-parameter handling
title: Environmental linkages and priors: a formula-driven API
text: three species × two sexes × ~ temp (intercept + slope) pooled table 12 rows – (Intercept) temp slope per (species, sex). Priors inits supplied (Intercept) flow base parameter (K, M1, R0, …); slope rows hold year--year offset combines base. exact behavior depends whether formula carries intercept: Intercept-bearing formulas (~ 1, ~ temp) – base parameter remains estimable; example R0 species s lives rec_pars[s, 1] exactly without linkages. (Intercept) row table exists bookkeeping hook init/prior (see ) beta_linkage slot held 0 estimated. recruitment / mortality / growth modules read base + offset(yr) year – intercept fixed zero, offset exactly slope contribution. Slope-formulas (~ 0 + temp) – (Intercept) row, base parameter mapped (NA) stays default initial value, value supplied inits argument fit_mod, value supplied init = list("(Intercept)"= ...) spec.

previous_headings: Behind the scenes: automatic base-parameter handling
title: Environmental linkages and priors: a formula-driven API
text: init = list((Intercept)= X) linkage spec flows base parameter rather linkage row. linkage row’s beta_linkage slot stays 0; base parameter starts X. recommended way set sensible starting value intercept-bearing linkages – composes naturally phasing (base parameter goes existing per-process phase logic) keeps optimiser grounded.
code: # Start M1 at 0.06 without estimating an extra intercept beta. build_M1(   M1_model = "sex_age_invariant",   linkages = list(     M1 = linkage_spec(       formula = ~ 1,       init    = list(`(Intercept)` = 0.06)     )   ) )

previous_headings: Behind the scenes: automatic base-parameter handling
title: Environmental linkages and priors: a formula-driven API
text: Stratification () determines base-parameter slots affected: = ~ species produces one (Intercept) row per species; = NULL (fully shared linkage) produces single shared row; = ~ species + sex produces one per (species, sex). (Intercept) row user supplies init pushes init matching base-parameter slot. rule applies uniformly every linkage target (K, L1, Linf, m, M1, R0, alpha, beta).

title: Environmental linkages and priors: a formula-driven API
text: model single-sex (nsex = 1 every species scope), asking = ~ species + sex produces warning: one sex level available, sex stratum collapses single shared level. result equivalent = ~ species. Models mixed nsex (single-sex, two-sex species) emit one sex level per species automatically – single-sex species get one row per parameter, two-sex species get two.

title: Environmental linkages and priors: a formula-driven API
text: Random-effects grouping – re_group column linkage table stored end--end; cpp grow hierarchical penalty coefficients sharing re_group value partially pooled. Age-dependent linkages processes M – age_bin stratum consumed M accumulator today (row’s age_bin == NA broadcasts across ages; specific values pin offset age slice). schema reserved processes may eventually vary age. Selectivity / catchability linkages – encoder already reserves process = "sel" process = "q" codes, cpp accumulator consumes yet. Legacy retirement – srr_indices, M1_indices, srr_fun %% c(1, 3, 5), M1_model %% c(4, 5) deprecated; see migration table NEWS.md.

what: Build a growth model with linkages
title: Growth estimation with linkages and priors
text: Rceattle supports growth linkages build_growth() linkage_spec(). linkage table can alter von Bertalanffy growth parameter K, Linf, L1 (natural-scale names; default link = "log" keeps underlying TMB parameter log scale), can also carry priors linked coefficients.
code: # Create a simple environmental covariate for the example data. set.seed(123) yrs <- whamGrowthData$styr:whamGrowthData$endyr whamGrowthData$env_data <- data.frame(   Year = yrs,   temp = rnorm(length(yrs), 0, 0.5) )   growth_spec <- build_growth(   fun = "vonBertalanffy",   linkages = list(     Linf = linkage_spec(       formula = ~ temp,             # 2 columns: (Intercept) and `temp`       by      = ~ species,          # one beta per (species, column)       priors  = list(         # Intercept prior is on natural-scale Linf (log link back-transforms).         # Use lognormal() if you want a Normal on log(Linf) instead.         "(Intercept)" = normal(85, 5),         temp = normal(0, 0.1)) # Tight prior on the slope     )   ) )

title: Growth estimation with linkages and priors
text: formula = ~ temp fits intercept temperature slope. = ~ species gives species intercept slope (add + sex split sex). link = "log" (default) keeps underlying TMB parameter log scale, slope rows act multiplicatively natural Linf. priors attaches Normal prior intercept temperature slope. prior (Intercept) effectively prior base Linf value (natural scale, default log link back-transformed inside prior block), intercept-bearing linkages replace base parameter carry level.

title: 1. Rceattle: An Introduction
text: vignette fits sequence five single- multi-species models Rceattle, applied walleye pollock, arrowtooth flounder, Pacific cod Gulf Alaska eastern Bering Sea. model follows Holsman et al. (2016) Adams et al. (2022). Every function help available via ?. workflow : Install Rceattle Load Rceattle associated excel data Fit assessment models: model 1: single-species assessment model estimated recruitment estimated penalized effects; model 2: three single-species assessment models jointly estimated recruitment estimated penalized effects; model 3: model 2, natural mortality estimated species; model 4: model 3, recruitment estimated random effects; model 5: full multi-species assessment models time- age- varying natural mortality due predation. Compare models AIC Mohn’s rho (retrospective analysis) Review plots input data, diagnostics, results.

title: 1. Rceattle: An Introduction
text: Models fit fit_mod function. first model single-species fit stock–recruit relationship Gulf Alaska pollock. 8 fleets: 1 fishery, 6 surveys, 1 fleet turned (data excluded likelihood; see model_1$fleet_control). second model fits three single-species models jointly, stock–recruit curve natural mortality fixed input values (mydata$M1_base). 7 fleets: 3 fisheries (one per species) 4 surveys (see mydata$fleet_control). Single-species mode default (msmMode = 0): Alternatively, natural mortality can estimated build_M1 function; M1_model = "sex_age_invariant" estimates single M per species, constant across sex age: estimate model_4 recruitment treated random effects can use random_rec argument. model initialized previous model’s MLEs don’t phase estimation decrease run-time: estimate time- age-varying natural mortality due predation can estimate model multi-species mode setting msmMode = 1. follows MSVPA parameterization described Magnusson (1995).

No random recruitment                             fit_control = fit_control(                               phase = TRUE,                               verbose = 1)) summary(model_1) model_2 <- Rceattle::fit_mod(data_list = mydata,                             inits = NULL, # Initial parameters = 0                             estimateMode = 0, # Estimate                             random_rec = FALSE, # No random recruitment                             msmMode = 0, # Single-species                             fit_control = fit_control(                               phase = TRUE,                               verbose = 1)) summary(model_2) model_3 <- Rceattle::fit_mod(data_list = mydata,                               estimateMode = 0, # Estimate                               M1Fun = build_M1(M1_model = "sex_age_invariant"), # Estimate sex-invariant M)                               random_rec = FALSE, # Penalized likelihood                               msmMode = 0, # Single species mode                               fit_control = fit_control(                                 phase = TRUE,                                 verbose = 1)) summary(model_3) model_4 <- Rceattle::fit_mod(data_list = mydata,                               inits = model_3$estimated_params, # Start estimation at model 3's MLEs                               estimateMode = 0, # Estimate                               M1Fun = build_M1(M1_model = "sex_age_invariant"),                               random_rec = TRUE, # Random recruitment                               msmMode = 0, # Single species mode                               fit_control = fit_control(                                 phase = FALSE,                                 verbose = 1)) summary(model_4) model_5 <- Rceattle::fit_mod(data_list = BS2017MS,                             inits = model_3$estimated_params, # Initial parameters from single species estimates                             M1Fun = build_M1(M1_model = "sex_age_invariant"),                             estimateMode = 0, # Estimate                             niter = 3, # 3 iterations around population and predation dynamics                             random_rec = FALSE, # No random recruitment                             msmMode = 1, # MSVPA based                             suitMode = 0, # title: 1. Rceattle: An Introduction
text: Various plots diagnostics built Rceattle. Specifically, time-series hindcast forecast biomass, SSB, recruitment, biomass consumed prey, mortality--age, depletion uncertainty. time-series plots can accept list models (see ). Diagnostics plots include plotting selectivity, fits composition data, index fit, catch fit. Selectivity composition plot functions can input one model. Index catch fit plots can take multiple model inputs. Outputs model can queried using $ sign: model_1$initial_params - list initial parameter values prior estimation model_1$bounds - list parameter bounds model_1$map - list parameter map factor form (model_1$map$mapFactor) list form (model_1$map$mapList) model_1$estimated_params - list estimated parameters post estimation model_1$quantities - list derived quantities (SSB, biomass, selectivity, etc) model_1$data_list - input data model_1$run_time - model run time model_1$obj - TMB makeadfun object. model_1$opt - fit_tmb optimization object. model_1$sdrep - TMB sdreport object.

title: 3. Model diagnostics
text: Fitting model

title: 3. Model diagnostics
text: fit_mod() runs battery convergence checks optimization attaches result model$convergence. check one record severity ("OK", "NOTE", "WARN", "FAIL"); object’s status worst severity present. Non-OK checks surfaced via message() fit (non-converged model never turned error — fit always returned diagnostics attached), print(model) shows overall status. Re-run battery fit convergence_diagnostics(): checks cover: max_gradient — maximum absolute marginal gradient parameter carrying (WARN > 1e-3, FAIL > 1). pdHess — whether Hessian positive definite (FAIL ). sdreport_failed — FAIL sdreport requested Hessian inverted. hessian_conditioning — Hessian condition number , poorly conditioned, parameters loading least-identified direction (unidentified linear combination). Complements TMBhelper::check_estimability (per-parameter verdict) continuous severity direction. parameters_on_bounds — parameters hit configured build_bounds() limit (often unidentified mis-scaled). phasing — phases ended high gradient, localizing parameter block hard fit. estimability — surfaces TMBhelper::check_estimability ran.
code: model_1$convergence            # overall status + any non-OK checks print(model_1$convergence, all = TRUE)   # show every check, including OK ones convergence_diagnostics(model_1)

title: 3. Model diagnostics
text: Pearson residuals composition data standard normal even model correct, age/length bins correlated (fish one bin means fewer another) random effects induce correlation across years. One-step-ahead (OSA) residuals fix : observation residualized conditional previously-added observations, integrating random effects, residuals iid standard normal correctly specified model (Thygesen et al. 2017; Trijoulet et al. 2023). therefore support objective goodness--fit testing. osa_residuals() computes post hoc combination fitted data types – survey indices, fishery catch, age/length composition ("comp"), conditional age--length ("caal"), predator diet ("diet"). Composition data residualized conditional binomial / beta-binomial decomposition. OSA re-optimizes random effects per observation, expensive; run converged fit (estimateMode < 3). OSA sources – aggregate index/catch composition ("comp"/"caal"/"diet") – available fit; osa_residuals() builds required observation data demand. Following Stewart Monnahan (2025), practical workflow : Inspect aggregate fit across years (plot_comp(model_1)): systematic lack fit points structural misspecification (e.g. wrong selectivity shape). Compare SDNR null interval (osa_diagnostics()): value outside interval flags - -dispersion, often data-weighting effective-sample-size issue. Compare lower/upper tail statistics null intervals: localize departures tails residual distribution. Inspect Pearson bubble plots (plot_comp(model_1), default): patterns sign residuals across age/year can identify lack fit occurs – Stewart Monnahan recommend keeping alongside OSA residuals. Revise model data weighting misspecification found, using together diagnostics rather accept/reject test. OSA residuals discrete composition data randomized quantile residuals, stochastic; osa_residuals() takes seed reproducibility.
code: # Aggregate (catch + index) residuals osa <- osa_residuals(model_1, source = c("index", "catch")) head(osa)  # Statistical diagnostics (Stewart & Monnahan 2025): SDNR and lower/upper tail # statistics, each with the interval expected under the standard-normal null. osa_diagnostics(osa)  # Q-Q plot (with SDNR / tail annotation) + residual-by-year plot(osa)  # residuals() also exposes them in the common residual schema (`source` selects # the data, like `type` in stats::residuals.glm()): residuals(model_1, type = "osa", source = c("index", "catch"))  # Composition OSA residuals -- no special fit required plot_comp(model_1, residual_type = "osa")              # Q-Q + signed bubbles residuals(model_1, type = "osa", source = "comp")

title: 3. Model diagnostics
text: process_residuals() complementary check process model: standardizes model’s random-effect deviations (recruitment, initial abundance, catchability) process prior, drawing joint posterior (SAM’s procres; Nielsen Berg 2014). correct process model also approximately iid standard normal.
code: pr <- process_residuals(model_1, process = "recruitment") osa_diagnostics(pr) plot(pr)  # residuals() exposes them too: residuals(model_1, type = "process")

title: 3. Model diagnostics
text: retrospective analysis systematically removes recent years data one peel time re-fits model. Bias final estimates relative earlier peels summarised Mohn’s rho: values outside ±0.2 (SSB) generally indicate problem worth investigating. retrospective() function returns list two elements: nyrs_forecast argument (default 3) additionally evaluates rho years projected beyond terminal peel, making possible quantify forecast skill alongside retrospective bias single call.
code: model_1_retro <- retrospective(Rceattle = model_1, peels = 5)  # Mohn's rho for each quantity model_1_retro$mohns  # Plot historical trajectories across peels plot_biomass(model_1_retro$Rceattle_list)  # Include the projection period to see how the forecast changes plot_biomass(model_1_retro$Rceattle_list, incl_proj = TRUE)

title: 3. Model diagnostics
text: Jitter testing re-fits model many randomly perturbed starting values check whether optimizer consistently returns minimum negative log-likelihood (NLL). spread NLL values across jitters suggests likelihood surface multiple local minima results interpreted cautiously. Non-converging runs silently dropped Rceattle_list, length(jitters$Rceattle_list) much less njitter, convergence may fragile. retrospective() jitter() fit peels / starts parallel default. Pass cores = 1 force sequential execution; otherwise call uses PSOCK cluster sized parallel::detectCores() - 6 (capped 2 R CMD check).
code: jitters <- jitter(Rceattle = model_1, njitter = 10, phase = TRUE)  # default njitter = 50  # Histogram of NLL differences relative to the best run hist(log(jitters$nll - min(jitters$nll)),      main = "Jitter NLL spread (log scale)",      xlab = "log(NLL - min NLL)")  # Overlay biomass trajectories — tight overlap indicates a stable optimum plot_biomass(jitters$Rceattle_list)  # Number of runs that converged length(jitters$Rceattle_list)

title: 3. Model diagnostics
text: self_test() simulates nsim datasets fitted model — keeping estimated parameters fixed — re-fits model simulated dataset. estimates refits cluster around parameter values fit simulated , model least self-consistent (can recover estimates data generated). Persistent bias wide spread quantity sign data informative . simulation uses seed + RNG seed, results reproducible whether cores > 1. Set simulate = FALSE refit model’s expected values (observation error) rather draws observation likelihood — useful confirming estimator returns generating parameters noise-free limit. cores behaves way retrospective() jitter().
code: sims <- self_test(model_1, nsim = 10)            # default nsim = 50  # Number of simulations that converged (non-converged runs are dropped) length(sims)  # Overlay biomass / SSB trajectories across simulations — the original fit's # trajectory should sit inside the spread of the refits. plot_biomass(c(list(model_1), sims), model_names = c("fit", names(sims))) plot_ssb(c(list(model_1), sims),     model_names = c("fit", names(sims)))

title: 3. Model diagnostics
text: profile() re-fits model across grid fixed values chosen parameter returns resulting NLL surface. flat profile means data carry little information parameter; sharp minimum away MLE means fit actually settled . supports recruitment standard deviation, stock–recruit parameters, natural mortality. Specify parameter natural-scale alias: "sigmaR" (recruitment standard deviation), "M1" (natural mortality), stock–recruit parameters "R0", "alpha", "beta". Aliases take natural-scale values directly. slots gives cell(s) profile — usually just species index — values gives grid values . Supplying one slot profiles full grid combinations. profile() returns Rceattle_list (one fit per grid row, NULL fit failed), grid (user-scale value grid), nll (joint NLL aligned grid, NA non-converged fits), echoes param slots. cross-profile across multiple species, supply one slot per species (e.g. slots = list(1, 2, 3) param = "sigmaR"); cross-profile M1 across sex, supply one slot per sex third example . cores behaves way diagnostic functions.
code: # 1-D profile: sigmaR for species 1 (natural-scale alias) prof_sigmaR <- profile(   fitted = model_1,   param    = "sigmaR",   slots    = list(1),   values   = list(seq(0.1, 1.5, by = 0.1)) )  plot(prof_sigmaR$grid$slot_1,      prof_sigmaR$nll - min(prof_sigmaR$nll, na.rm = TRUE),      type = "l", xlab = "sigmaR", ylab = "dNLL")  # 1-D profile: SRR alpha for species 1 # (alias fills in the rec_pars column; slot is just the species index) prof_alpha <- profile(   fitted = model_1,   param    = "alpha",   slots    = list(1),   values   = list(seq(2, 80, length.out = 20)) )  # 2-D cross-profile: M1 across sex for species 1, age 1 prof_M_sex <- profile(   fitted = model_1,   param    = "M1",   slots    = list(c(1, 1, 1), c(1, 2, 1)),  # males and females   values   = list(seq(0.10, 0.40, by = 0.05),                   seq(0.10, 0.40, by = 0.05)) )

text: Multiple age-based selectivity functions supported Rceattle. controlled Selectivity_index, Selectivity, N_sel_bins, Time_varying_sel, Time_varying_sel_sd_prior, Bin_first_selected fleet_control sheet Rceattle data file. defined follows: Selectivity_index: index use selectivities different surveys Selectivity: Selectivity parameterization use species: 0 = empirical selectivity provided srv_emp_sel; 1 = logistic selectivity; 2 = non-parametric selecitivty sensu Ianelli et al 2018; 3 = double logistic; 4 = descending logistic; 5 = non-parametric selectivity sensu Taylor et al 2014 (Hake), 6 “2DAR1” age year, 7 “3DAR1” sensu Cheng et al (2025). Time_varying_sel_sd_prior: sd use random walk time varying selectivity set 1. Bin_first_selected: Age/length bin selectivity non-zero. Selectivity age set 0.

Catchability = 5, determines environmental index used equation log(q_y) = q_mu + beta * index_y Time_varying_q_sd_prior sd use random walk time varying q set 1

title: 4. Projections and reference points
code: library(Rceattle)  data(BS2017SS) data(BS2017MS)  # Set the terminal projection year BS2017SS$projyr <- 2060 BS2017MS$projyr <- 2060  # Plot input data plot_data(BS2017SS)  # Fit baseline single- and multi-species models ss_run <- fit_mod(   data_list    = BS2017SS,   inits        = NULL,   file         = NULL,   estimateMode = 0,   random_rec   = FALSE,   msmMode      = 0,   fit_control = fit_control(     phase        = TRUE,     verbose      = 1))  ms_run <- fit_mod(   data_list    = BS2017MS,   inits        = ss_run$estimated_params,   file         = NULL,   estimateMode = 0,   niter        = 5,   random_rec   = FALSE,   msmMode      = 1,   suitMode     = 0,   fit_control = fit_control(     verbose      = 1))

title: 4. Projections and reference points
text: estimateMode = 2 runs projection period (holding estimated parameters fixed) specified harvest control rule. build_hcr(HCR = 2, Ftarget = ...) sets constant F species. proj_F_prop column fleet_control controls projected F split across fleets multiple fisheries targeting species (values must sum 1 per species).
code: BS2017MS$fleet_control$proj_F_prop <- 1  # One fishery fleet per species  ms_run_proj <- fit_mod(   data_list    = BS2017MS,   inits        = ms_run$estimated_params,   file         = NULL,   estimateMode = 2,   HCR          = build_hcr(HCR = "ConstantF",                             Ftarget = c(0.2342936, 0.513, 0.0774777)),   niter        = 5,   random_rec   = FALSE,   msmMode      = 1,   suitMode     = 0,   fit_control = fit_control(     verbose      = 1))  plot_catch(ms_run_proj, incl_proj = TRUE)

title: 4. Projections and reference points
text: Projection recruitment deviations stored parameter list can replaced directly forward-projection run. estimateMode = 3 evaluates model without re-estimating parameters, updated recruitment deviations affect projection.
code: nyrs      <- BS2017MS$endyr - BS2017MS$styr + 1 nyrs_proj <- BS2017MS$projyr - BS2017MS$styr + 1 yrs_proj  <- (nyrs + 1):nyrs_proj  # Replace future rec_devs with draws from N(0, 0.707) ms_run$estimated_params$rec_dev[, yrs_proj] <- stats::rnorm(   n    = length(ms_run$estimated_params$rec_dev[, yrs_proj]),   mean = 0,   sd   = 0.707 )  ms_run_proj2 <- fit_mod(   data_list    = BS2017MS,   inits        = ms_run$estimated_params,   file         = NULL,   estimateMode = 3,   # Evaluate only — do not re-estimate   niter        = 5,   random_rec   = FALSE,   msmMode      = 1,   suitMode     = 0,   fit_control = fit_control(     verbose      = 1))

title: 4. Projections and reference points
text: sample_rec() bootstraps historical recruitment deviations projection period. optional rec_trend argument adds linear trend: rec_trend = -0.5 imposes 50% decline mean recruitment end projection.
code: ms_run_proj3 <- sample_rec(   Rceattle     = ms_run,   sample_rec   = TRUE,   update_model = TRUE,   rec_trend    = -0.5   # 50% decline in mean recruitment )

title: 4. Projections and reference points
code: mod_list  <- list(ms_run, ms_run_proj, ms_run_proj2, ms_run_proj3) mod_names <- c(   "No fishing",   "Constant F",   "Stochastic recruitment",   "Declining recruitment" )  plot_biomass(Rceattle = mod_list, model_names = mod_names, incl_proj = TRUE) plot_recruitment(Rceattle = mod_list, model_names = mod_names, incl_proj = TRUE) plot_catch(Rceattle = mod_list, model_names = mod_names, incl_proj = TRUE)

title: 4. Projections and reference points
text: Setting random_rec = TRUE treats log-recruitment deviations random effects marginalised via Laplace approximation rather penalised fixed effects. propagates process uncertainty projections automatically.
code: ss_re <- fit_mod(   data_list    = BS2017SS,   inits        = NULL,   file         = NULL,   estimateMode = 0,   random_rec   = TRUE,   msmMode      = 0,   fit_control = fit_control(     phase        = FALSE,     verbose      = 1))  # Compare fixed vs. random effects recruitment uncertainty plot_recruitment(   Rceattle    = list(ss_run, ss_re),   model_names = c("Fixed effects", "Random effects"),   add_ci      = TRUE )

title: 4. Projections and reference points
text: HCR argument fit_mod() accepts output build_hcr(). See ?build_hcr full parameter details. closed-loop testing control rules across many simulated trajectories, see vignette("hcrs--mses").
code: # Example: NPFMC Tier 3 control rule (single-species only) ss_run_tier3 <- fit_mod(   data_list    = BS2017SS,   inits        = ss_run$estimated_params,   file         = NULL,   estimateMode = 2,   HCR          = build_hcr(HCR = "NPFMC",                             Ftarget = 0.40,   # F40%                             Flimit  = 0.35,   # F35%                             Ptarget = 0.40,                             Plimit  = 0.20,                             Alpha   = 0.05),   random_rec   = FALSE,   msmMode      = 0,   fit_control = fit_control(     verbose      = 1))

title: 5. Single- vs. multi-species models
text: Single-species appropriate : Predation interactions unknown negligible species interest major predators prey system building initial model debugging data inputs Multi-species appropriate : Predation important source mortality (e.g., groundfish Bering Sea Gulf Alaska) want evaluate climate-driven changes predator prey abundance propagate food web Reference points account ecosystem effects common workflow fit single-species models first use estimates starting values (inits) multi-species run.

title: 5. Single- vs. multi-species models
text: niter argument controls many times population dynamics predation mortality equations iterated convergence within gradient step. Five iterations typically sufficient.
code: library(Rceattle)  # BS2017SS and BS2017MS use the same data structure but differ in M1_base: # the multi-species dataset has lower residual mortality because some of # that mortality is explained by predation (M2) in multi-species mode. data(BS2017SS) data(BS2017MS) BS2017SS$projyr <- 2060 BS2017MS$projyr <- 2060  plot_data(BS2017SS) # Single-species ss_run <- fit_mod(   data_list    = BS2017SS,   inits        = NULL,   file         = NULL,   estimateMode = 0,   random_rec   = FALSE,   msmMode      = 0, # <-- single-species   fit_control = fit_control(     phase        = TRUE,     verbose      = 1))  # Multi-species — start from single-species MLEs for stability ms_run <- fit_mod(   data_list    = BS2017MS,   inits        = ss_run$estimated_params,  # warm start   file         = NULL,   estimateMode = 0,   niter        = 5,        # iterations between population and predation dynamics   random_rec   = FALSE,   msmMode      = 1,        # <-- Type II MSVPA   suitMode     = 0, # empirical suitability from diet data   fit_control = fit_control(     verbose      = 1))

title: 5. Single- vs. multi-species models

code: data("GOA2018SS") plot_data(GOA2018SS)  # Single-species goa_ss <- fit_mod(   data_list    = GOA2018SS,   inits        = NULL,   file         = NULL,   estimateMode = 0,   random_rec   = FALSE,   msmMode      = 0,   fit_control = fit_control(     phase        = TRUE,     verbose      = 1))  # Single-species with estimated M goa_ss_M <- fit_mod(   data_list    = GOA2018SS,   inits        = goa_ss$estimated_params,   file         = NULL,   estimateMode = 0,   M1Fun        = build_M1(M1_model = c(1, 2, 1)),  # Estimate M: single M for spp 1 & 3, sex-specific for spp 2   random_rec   = FALSE,   msmMode      = 0,   fit_control = fit_control(     phase        = TRUE,     verbose      = 1))  # Multi-species goa_ms <- fit_mod(   data_list    = GOA2018SS,   inits        = goa_ss$estimated_params,   file         = NULL,   estimateMode = 0,   M1Fun        = build_M1(M1_model = c(1, 2, 1)),   niter        = 3,   random_rec   = FALSE,   msmMode      = 1,   suitMode     = 0,   fit_control = fit_control(     phase        = TRUE,     verbose      = 1))

code: mod_list  <- list(ss_run, ms_run) mod_names <- c("Single-species", "Multi-species")  # Population trajectories plot_biomass(Rceattle = mod_list, model_names = mod_names) plot_ssb(Rceattle = mod_list, model_names = mod_names) plot_recruitment(Rceattle = mod_list, model_names = mod_names, add_ci = TRUE) plot_depletionSSB(Rceattle = mod_list, model_names = mod_names)  # Mortality breakdown (M1 vs M2) — these accept model lists plot_m_at_age(Rceattle = mod_list, model_names = mod_names, age = 2) plot_m2_at_age_prop(Rceattle = mod_list, model_names = mod_names)  # plot_mortality() accepts only a single model; call separately per model plot_mortality(ms_run)   # tile plot of total mortality-at-age across years plot_mortality(ms_run, type = 2)  # facet line version plot_mortality(ms_run, M2 = FALSE) # total M (M1 + M2); M2 = TRUE plots M2 only  # Predation (multi-species only) — these also accept single models only plot_b_eaten(Rceattle = mod_list, model_names = mod_names) plot_b_eaten_prop(Rceattle = mod_list, model_names = mod_names)
